strengths: Novel and well-motivated integration of higher-order topological structures (cell/simplicial complexes) into a diffusion-bridge-based coarse-to-fine graph generation curriculum, addressing genuine limitations of adapting image-diffusion frameworks to graphs (rapid degradation to uniform noise, loss of sparsity/connectivity).

Provides theoretical analysis (faster score-matching convergence via PL-condition argument, tighter reconstruction error bounds via Gronwall's inequality) that is reasonably well worked out in the appendix with full derivations for the diffusion bridge (generalized OU process via Doob's h-transform).

Strong and broad empirical evaluation across five datasets (QM9, ZINC250k, Community-small, Enzymes, Ego-small) against a large set of autoregressive, flow-based, GAN, and diffusion baselines, showing state-of-the-art or highly competitive results on most metrics, especially large gains in NSPDK/FCD on ZINC250k.

Thoughtful ablation study comparing Cell/Peripheral/Noise guides that empirically supports the theoretical claims and offers interpretability insight into which topological information drives performance.
Comprehensive appendix including complexity analysis of cell/simplex filtering, architecture details, training/sampling algorithms, and extensive qualitative visualizations.
weaknesses: The theoretical claims rely on fairly strong/idealized assumptions (β-smoothness, µ-PL condition, Lipschitz score functions, modeling the coarse-to-fine intermediate corruption as simple additive Gaussian noise x' = x + ε) that may not accurately reflect the actual cell-filtering-based corruption process used in practice, weakening the rigor of the 'sharper bound' claims.

Novelty scores drop substantially compared to baselines on QM9 (75.12 vs. ~85-100 for most other methods) and are also slightly lower on ZINC250k, suggesting a diversity/novelty trade-off that is not discussed or analyzed by the authors.

The method's advantage appears data-dependent: the paper itself notes only modest gains on Ego-small due to sparse higher-order structure, raising questions about applicability to graphs without rich higher-order topology (e.g., trees, sparse random graphs).
No ablation on the number of hierarchical steps K (experiments fixed at K=2), leaving open how sensitive performance is to this design choice or whether more granular curricula would help.
No error bars, multiple-run variance, or significance testing reported in the main results tables, making it hard to assess robustness of the reported improvements.

Limited discussion of computational overhead relative to baselines (the denoising network combines GCN, Attention, and FiLM modules, plus preprocessing for cell/simplex filtering), despite an appendix complexity analysis; no wall-clock/training-time comparison against baselines is provided in the main text.

The claimed novelty of 'first to consider higher-order guides for graph generation' is somewhat strong given cell/simplex filtering is a relatively simple heuristic (cycle/clique extraction) rather than a deeper exploitation of higher-order topological learning methods.

strengths: The core idea of using higher-order topological structures (cell/simplicial complexes) to define a coarse-to-fine generation curriculum for graph diffusion is conceptually interesting and addresses a real limitation of prior image-inspired diffusion frameworks for graphs.

The integration of a generalized Ornstein-Uhlenbeck diffusion bridge (via Doob's h-transform) with spectral (Laplacian eigenvalue) diffusion is a reasonable technical combination that respects permutation equivariance and graph sparsity concerns.

The paper provides theoretical analysis (faster score-matching convergence, tighter reconstruction error bounds) with fairly detailed proofs in the appendix, which is uncommon rigor for this application area.
Experiments span both molecular (QM9, ZINC250k) and generic graph (Community-small, Ego-small, Enzymes) benchmarks with an extensive set of standard baselines.
Ablation study on different topological guides (cell vs. peripheral vs. noise) provides some empirical support for the theoretical claims and offers interpretability insight.
Visualizations of the coarse-to-fine generation trajectory are informative and illustrate the intended mechanism clearly.
weaknesses: A highly relevant and recent baseline, GruM (Jo et al., 2024), which also uses an OU-type diffusion bridge for graph generation, is discussed in related work but omitted from experimental comparison, leaving open whether the higher-order guidance itself (rather than just the bridge formulation) drives the reported gains.

Results are not uniformly state-of-the-art: on QM9 the novelty score drops sharply to 75.12 (worse than GDSS's 86.27 and most baselines except DiGress), and this concerning side-effect (possible mode collapse toward training-like structures) is not analyzed or discussed. On Enzymes, HOG-Diff is not best on Deg. or Clus. metrics (DiGress and GDSS outperform it there), contradicting the abstract's claim of consistently outperforming or remaining competitive without deeper caveat.

The theoretical propositions rely on strong, only partially justified assumptions (β-smoothness, PL condition, Lipschitz score networks) and the comparison between HOG-Diff and a 'classical' model in Prop. 3.4 hinges on an informal argument (monotonicity of a(τ), b(τ)) that does not rigorously establish the claim for general neural network parameterizations used in practice.

Several core components (spectral/Laplacian eigenvalue diffusion, FiLM-based conditioning, GCN+Attention denoiser) are directly adapted from prior work (Luo et al. 2023a; Martinkus et al. 2022; Vignac et al. 2023), somewhat limiting the technical novelty beyond the higher-order guidance idea itself.

The ablation on topological guides is only conducted on the molecular datasets (QM9, ZINC250k); no equivalent ablation is shown for the generic graph datasets, despite the paper itself noting that guide choice is especially impactful for datasets like Ego-small with few higher-order structures.

No standard deviations or multiple-run statistics are reported for any experiment, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the reported improvements, several of which are numerically small.
The number of hierarchical windows K is fixed at 2 throughout all experiments with no ablation on this key hyperparameter, despite the framework being presented as generalizable to arbitrary K.

The claim of being 'the first to consider higher-order guides for graph generation' is somewhat overstated without deeper engagement with related hierarchical/coarse-to-fine or topology-aware generative approaches beyond the cited hypergraph-specific works.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea of incorporating higher-order topological structures (cell complexes/simplicial complexes) as intermediate guides in a coarse-to-fine diffusion generation curriculum, addressing a genuine gap between topological deep learning and generative modeling.

Principled technical construction using the generalized Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (GOU) diffusion bridge with closed-form transition probabilities, enabling simulation-free training and smooth transitions between coarse and fine intermediate graph states.

Theoretical contributions (Theorem 3 on faster score-matching convergence via smaller smoothness constant, Theorem 4 on tighter reconstruction error bounds) are provided with fairly detailed proofs, going beyond purely empirical justification common in this area.

Extensive empirical evaluation across both molecular (QM9, ZINC250k) and generic graph benchmarks (Community-small, Enzymes, Ego-small, SBM), with consistent or state-of-the-art results against a large and reasonably up-to-date set of baselines (including recent flow-matching methods like DeFoG and CatFlow).

Thoughtful ablation studies isolating the effect of the topological guide (cell vs. peripheral vs. noise), which directly supports the core hypothesis and links empirical behavior back to the theoretical claims.

Good engineering care regarding permutation invariance/equivariance, spectral-domain diffusion instead of raw adjacency matrix, and complexity/scalability analysis (including cell filtering complexity and sampling time comparisons).
weaknesses: The improvement over strong recent baselines like DeFoG is often numerically small (e.g., QM9 Val. w/o corr. and Novelty are actually worse than DeFoG; Ego-small results are only tied/comparable, not superior), somewhat undercutting the 'consistently outperforms' claim, and the paper itself acknowledges reduced benefit when higher-order structure is sparse.

The theoretical results rely on fairly strong/idealized assumptions (β-smoothness, µ-PL condition, sufficiently expressive score network, Lipschitz/boundedness assumptions, and a heuristic argument treating higher-order filtering as equivalent to Gaussian noise injection for the smoothness comparison) that may not rigorously hold in practice, making the 'stronger theoretical guarantee' claim somewhat overstated relative to what is rigorously shown.

The choice of K=2 stages and specific filtering dimension (2-cell vs 3-simplex) appears heuristic/dataset-specific (justified post-hoc via data statistics in appendix), raising questions about generality and the sensitivity of results to this design choice; no systematic study of K>2 or automatic selection of guide type is provided.

Some baselines/comparisons lack standard deviations or are taken from other papers without re-running under identical conditions (marked with asterisks), and a few cells are missing (e.g., '-'), which slightly weakens the rigor of comparisons.

The molecular generation gains are partly attributable to standard tricks already used by prior spectral/Laplacian diffusion works (e.g., GSDM, DeFoG), so the incremental contribution specifically attributable to higher-order guidance versus other architectural/training choices (unified GCN+Attention score network, spectral domain) is not fully disentangled.

Novelty metric on ZINC250k is essentially saturated for most baselines at ~100% while HOG-Diff scores notably lower (99.53%), and on QM9 HOG-Diff's novelty (75.12%) is substantially lower than many baselines, which is not thoroughly discussed as a potential trade-off of the coarse-to-fine higher-order guidance approach.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and relatively underexplored gap: explicitly incorporating higher-order topological structures (cell/simplicial complexes) into diffusion-based graph generation, rather than treating graphs as generic Euclidean data.

The coarse-to-fine curriculum implemented via a generalized Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (GOU) diffusion bridge is a reasonable and technically coherent instantiation of the idea, with closed-form transition probabilities enabling simulation-free training.

Extensive empirical evaluation spans both molecular (QM9, ZINC250k) and generic graph benchmarks (Community-small, Ego-small, Enzymes, SBM), with the method achieving state-of-the-art or competitive results on most metrics.

Useful ablations comparing different topological guides (noise vs. peripheral structures vs. cell-based guides) and diffusion domains (adjacency vs. Laplacian spectrum) that support some of the design choices and add a degree of interpretability.
Thorough appendix with proofs, complexity analysis, dataset statistics, and visualizations, suggesting reasonable reproducibility effort.
weaknesses: The theoretical results (Theorems 3 and 4) rely on an informal and somewhat contrived reduction: to compare smoothness/Lipschitz constants between HOG-Diff and 'classical' diffusion, the proof models the higher-order guided intermediate state as simply 'x plus isotropic Gaussian noise', which does not actually reflect the cell-complex filtering mechanism used in practice. This creates a significant gap between what is proven and what the method actually does, weakening the claimed theoretical guarantees.

The core technical building blocks (GOU/OU bridge processes, Doob's h-transform, spectral/Laplacian diffusion) are largely adapted from existing works (Luo et al. 2023a/b; Yue et al. 2024; Martinkus et al. 2022), and the main novelty is the combination with cell-complex filtering as a curriculum signal — a comparatively incremental engineering contribution rather than a fundamentally new generative technique.

Empirical gains over the strongest baselines (e.g., DeFoG) are often modest (e.g., QM9 FCD 0.172 vs 0.268; NSPDK 0.0003 vs 0.0005), and on generic graph datasets (Enzymes, Ego-small) improvements over DiGress/GDSS are marginal or absent, which the authors themselves attribute to insufficient higher-order structure — an important limitation that constrains the generality of the claimed contribution.

The choice of topological filter (2-cell vs. 3-simplex) differs by task and appears tuned post-hoc per dataset rather than derived from a principled, generalizable rule, raising concerns about how the method would generalize to new domains without extensive trial-and-error.

Only K=2 hierarchical stages are used throughout, with no ablation on the number of coarse-to-fine stages or sensitivity to the choice of window boundaries (τ_k), leaving an important design dimension unexplored.

Sampling time results (Table 4) are inconsistent (HOG-Diff slower than DiGress on Community-small but much faster on Enzymes) without a clear explanation, undermining confidence in the efficiency claims.
Novelty scores on ZINC250k (99.53) are lower than most baselines (many at or near 100.00), hinting at potential mode-coverage trade-offs not discussed in the main text.

The framework's reliance on preprocessing (lifting + filtering) is claimed to be efficient, but scalability is only demonstrated on relatively small graphs (largest is SBM with <200 nodes); no experiments on substantially larger, real-world graphs are provided to support broader claims of practical significance.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea of using higher-order topological structures (cell complexes, simplicial complexes) as explicit coarse-to-fine guidance for graph diffusion generation, addressing a genuine gap in prior graph diffusion literature that mostly operates purely on pairwise edges.

The generalized OU diffusion bridge formulation is theoretically grounded, with detailed derivations (Doob's h-transform, closed-form transition probabilities) and a clear connection/generalization of the Brownian bridge as a special case.

Extensive empirical evaluation across eight benchmarks (QM9, ZINC250k, MOSES, GuacaMol, Community-small, Ego-small, Enzymes, SBM) spanning both molecular and generic graph domains, including large-scale datasets, which is broader than most competing papers.
Strong and consistent empirical results, particularly the sharp reductions in FCD/NSPDK on molecular benchmarks and competitive/state-of-the-art results on generic graph benchmarks.

Additional topological preservation analysis via curvature filtrations (Table 3) provides evidence beyond standard statistical metrics that the higher-order structure is actually better preserved, which is a nice complement to standard MMD/FCD metrics.

Reasonably thorough ablations (guide type: cell vs. peripheral vs. noise; diffusion domain: spectral vs. adjacency; filtering rationale) and complexity/efficiency analysis showing the one-time preprocessing cost is manageable and sampling/training times are competitive.
Theoretical claims (faster convergence, tighter reconstruction bounds) are supported with formal proofs in the appendix, going beyond hand-wavy justification common in many diffusion papers.
weaknesses: The theoretical results (Theorems 3 and 4) rely on several strong, somewhat informal assumptions (e.g., that HOG-Diff's score network can represent the same function class as the classical one while ignoring the coarse guide, or that noise-based intermediate distributions are dominated in a Lipschitz sense by CCF-based distributions); these are asserted rather than rigorously justified, and the practical relevance of the exponential convergence bound (which depends on an idealized PL condition rarely satisfied by deep networks) is unclear.

Lemma 6 essentially assumes the multi-stage decomposition can only match or outperform the single-stage classical objective by architectural containment, but this argument seems to gloss over the fact that HOG-Diff's per-stage networks receive additional side information (the coarse graph) not available to the classical model, so the comparison may not be entirely fair/well-posed as a measure of intrinsic model quality versus benefiting from extra input.

The choice of using only K=2 stages throughout experiments is not well justified against deeper hierarchies; no ablation systematically explores K>2 or alternative dimension choices beyond a brief discussion in Sec 4.4/F.4, despite the framework being presented as generalizable to multiple hierarchical windows.

Performance gains on datasets lacking higher-order structure (e.g., Ego-small) are marginal or tied with baselines, and the paper's own limitation section acknowledges this dependency, somewhat undermining the generality of the claimed contribution.

Some baseline comparisons in Table 1 and elsewhere use results copied from other papers with asterisks (no reported std), creating potential inconsistency in evaluation conditions across methods; it's unclear whether all baselines were retuned/rerun under identical experimental settings.

The improvement margins on several standard metrics (e.g., validity, uniqueness) are modest or occasionally worse than baselines (e.g., DeFoG has better FCD/NSPDK on some subsets is not the case, but novelty is sometimes lower for HOG-Diff), suggesting the overall gains, while real, are not uniformly dominant across all metrics.

The additional computational overhead of cell complex filtering/lifting, while argued to be a manageable one-time cost, still adds pipeline complexity and dataset-dependent tuning (e.g., choice of 2-cell vs 3-simplex filtering per dataset) that could hinder reproducibility and generalization to novel datasets without prior structural analysis.

The paper's readability suffers somewhat from dense theoretical notation and heavy reliance on appendix material for core derivations, which may limit accessibility for readers focused on the empirical contributions.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea of explicitly using higher-order topological structures (cell complexes/simplicial complexes) as intermediate generation targets in a coarse-to-fine diffusion curriculum, addressing a genuine gap between topological deep learning and graph generative modeling.

Technically elegant use of the generalized Ornstein-Uhlenbeck diffusion bridge with closed-form transition densities, enabling simulation-free training while conditioning on intermediate topological skeletons.

Very comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning eight benchmarks across molecular (QM9, ZINC250k, MOSES, GuacaMol) and generic graph domains (Community-small, Ego-small, Enzymes, SBM), which is broader coverage than most competing papers.
Additional topological-preservation analysis using curvature filtrations (Table 3) provides a meaningful, non-standard evaluation axis beyond typical MMD/FCD metrics.

Reasonable complexity/scalability analysis showing the one-time cell-filtering preprocessing cost is tractable even for million-scale datasets, and sampling/training times are competitive with baselines.
Ablation on different types of guides (cell vs. peripheral vs. noise) supports the qualitative claim that topologically meaningful guides matter more than generic noise.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim that HOG-Diff has a smaller smoothness constant (βHOG-Diff ≤ βclassical, Theorem 3) rests on modeling the higher-order-guided intermediate graph as literally x + Gaussian noise added to the clean graph (Appendix A.2). This is a strong and not well-justified simplification—cell complex filtering removes/prunes nodes and edges rather than adding isotropic noise—so the proof effectively reduces to a generic "less noise is easier to denoise" argument rather than a genuine topology-specific guarantee, undercutting the claimed novelty of the theoretical contribution.

Theorem 4's claim of a tighter reconstruction-error bound is conditioned on Lemma 6/Eq. 64, i.e., that the multi-stage curriculum's total score-matching loss does not exceed the classical single-stage loss. This premise is not proven in general but only checked post hoc on a single training curve (Fig. 4, K=2) for one dataset, making the "provably tighter bound" framing somewhat overstated relative to what is actually guaranteed.

The general K-stage framework is presented, but essentially all experiments use only K=2 (coarse+fine); there is no ablation varying K, so the practical benefit of the more elaborate multi-window curriculum formalism is not empirically substantiated.

Empirical gains are inconsistent across benchmarks: on QM9, HOG-Diff is not the best in Validity, Uniqueness, or Novelty (MiCaM, DiGress, GraphDF outperform it on those axes), and on Ego-small/Enzymes the improvement over DiGress/GDSS is marginal or a tie on average MMD, which somewhat undermines the paper's central message that higher-order guidance is uniformly a "powerful generative signal."

The claim of being "the first to consider higher-order guides for graph generation" is arguably overstated given closely related prior coarse-to-fine/hierarchical approaches (GPrinFlowNet's frequency curriculum, HiGen's hierarchical decomposition, HierDiff's fragment-level coarse-to-fine, and diffusion-bridge-based graph generation in GruM/Wu et al.), which the related-work section itself cites but does not sufficiently differentiate from in terms of conceptual novelty.

The diagnostic guide ablation (Table 4) validating the theoretical reconstruction-error ordering is only conducted on two molecular datasets (QM9, ZINC250k), not across the full suite of eight benchmarks, limiting the generality of the empirical support for the theory.

The rationale for filtering-dimension choice (2-cells for molecules, 3-simplices for generic graphs) is post hoc and dataset-specific, essentially tuned per domain, which raises questions about how a practitioner would select the appropriate order for a novel dataset without extensive trial and error—an issue the authors themselves flag as future work rather than resolve.
